{{Short description|School of thought}}
The '''Lwów–Warsaw School'''<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Bečvářová |editor1-first=Martina |title=Development Of Mathematics Between The World Wars: Case Studies, Examples And Analyses |date=2021 |publisher=[[World Scientific]] |isbn=9781786349309 |page=174}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Cohen |editor1-first=Robert S. |editor2-last=Schnelle |editor2-first=Thomas |title=Cognition and Fact: Materials on Ludwik Fleck |date=2011 |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |isbn=9789401085045 |pages=15-16, 217-218}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Sebeok |first1=Thomas A. |title=Encyclopedic Dictionary of Semiotics: Vol. 1; A-M |date=1986 |publisher=[[De Gruyter]] |isbn=0899251374 |pages=21, 144}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Stammerjohann |editor1-first=Harro |title=Lexicon Grammaticorum: A bio-bibliographical companion to the history of linguistics; Vol. 1 |date=2009 |publisher=[[Max Niemeyer Verlag]] |isbn=9783484730687 |pages=20 |edition=2nd}}</ref> ({{langx|pl|Szkoła Lwowsko-Warszawska}}) was an interdisciplinary [[school of thought|school]] (mainly philosophy, logic and psychology) founded by [[Kazimierz Twardowski]] in 1895 in [[Lviv|Lwów]], [[Austro-Hungary]] (now [[Lviv]], [[Ukraine]]).<ref>{{cite book |last=Rzepa |first=Teresa |chapter=Twardowski Kazimierz Jerzy Adolf ze Skrzypny Ogończyk |editor-last1=Kosnarewicz |editor-first1=Elwira |editor-last2=Rzepa |editor-first2=Teresa |editor-last3=Stachowski |editor-first3=Ryszard |display-editors=et al |title=Słownik psychologów polskich |language=pl |trans-title=Dictionary of Polish psychologists |publisher=Instytut Psychologii UAM |location=Poznań |year=1992 |pages=198–199 |oclc=834052536}}</ref>

Though its members represented a variety of disciplines, from [[mathematics]] through [[logic]] to [[psychology]], the Lwów–Warsaw School is widely considered to have been a philosophical movement.<ref>{{cite book |last=Woleński |first=Jan |title=Filozoficzna szkoła lwowsko-warszawska |trans-title=Lwów–Warsaw School of Philosophy |publisher=[[Polish Scientific Publishers PWN|PWN]] |location=Warsaw |year=1985 |page=5 |isbn=83-01-05334-8}}</ref> It has produced some of the leading [[logic]]ians of the twentieth century such as [[Jan Łukasiewicz]], [[Stanisław Leśniewski]], and [[Alfred Tarski]], among others.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Brentano|first=Franz|title=Psychology from An Empirical Standpoint|publisher=Routledge|year=2015|isbn=9781138019171|location=Oxon|pages=vii}}</ref> Its members did not only contribute to the techniques of logic but also to various domains that belong to the [[philosophy of language]].<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Kijania-Placek|first1=Katarzyna|title=The Lvov-Warsaw School and Contemporary Philosophy|last2=Wolenski|first2=Jan|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|year=2012|isbn=978-94-010-6146-9|location=Dordrecht|pages=219|language=en}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:Kazimierz Twardowski 1933.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Kazimierz Twardowski]]]]
Polish philosophy and the Lwów–Warsaw school were considerably influenced by [[Franz Brentano]] and his pupils Kazimierz Twardowski, [[Anton Marty]], [[Alexius Meinong]], and [[Edmund Husserl]]. Twardowski founded the philosophical school when he became the chair of the Lviv University.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Szumilewicz-Lachman|first=Irena|title=Zygmunt Zawirski: His Life and Work: with Selected Writings on Time, Logic and the Methodology of Science, Volume 157|publisher=Kluwer Academic Publishers|year=2012|isbn=978-0792325666|location=Dordrecht|pages=3}}</ref>

Principal topics of interest to the Lwów–Warsaw school included formal [[ontology]], [[mereology]], and universal or [[categorial grammar]].

The Lwów-Warsaw School began as a general philosophical school but steadily moved toward logic. The Lwów–Warsaw school of logic lay at the origin of ''[[Polish logic]]'' and was closely associated with or was part of the [[Warsaw School of Mathematics]]. According to [[Jan Woleński]], a decisive factor in the school's development was the view that the future of the Polish school of mathematics depended on the research connected with the new branches of the field such as [[set theory]] and [[topology]], which are closely related to mathematical logic.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Wolenski|first=Jan|title=Logic and Philosophy in the Lvov—Warsaw School|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|year=2012|isbn=978-94-010-7666-1|location=Dordrecht|pages=11, 18}}</ref> The "philosophical branch" followed Twardowski's tradition and produced notable thinkers such as [[Bronisław Bandrowski]], who addressed the problem of [[Inductive reasoning|induction]] and [[Tadeusz Kotarbiński]], who is known for developing [[Reism]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Krajewski|first=Władysław|title=Polish Philosophers of Science and Nature in the 20th Century|date=2001|publisher=Rodopi|isbn=90-420-1497-0|location=Amsterdam|pages=11}}</ref>

In the 1930s Alfred Tarski initiated contacts with the [[Vienna Circle]]. Tarski, the most prominent member of the Lwów–Warsaw School, has been ranked as one of the four greatest logicians of all time, along with [[Aristotle]], [[Gottlob Frege]], and [[Kurt Gödel]].<ref name="FF">[[#F-F|Feferman & Feferman]], p. 1</ref><ref name="Vaught">{{cite journal|last=Vaught|first=Robert L.|date=Dec 1986|title=Alfred Tarski's Work in Model Theory|journal=[[Journal of Symbolic Logic]]|publisher=ASL|volume=51|issue=4|pages=869–882|doi=10.2307/2273900|jstor=2273900}}</ref><ref name="Restall">{{cite web|url=http://consequently.org/writing/logicians/|title=Great Moments in Logic |last=Restall|first=Greg|date=2002–2006|access-date=2009-01-03| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20081206052240/http://consequently.org/writing/logicians/| archive-date= 6 December 2008 | url-status= live}}</ref>

The school's work was interrupted by the outbreak of [[World War II]].<ref name=":0" /> Despite this, its members went on to fundamentally influence modern science, notably [[mathematics]] and [[logic]], in the post-war period. Tarski's description of semantic truth, for instance, has revolutionized logic and philosophy.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Brożek|first1=Anna|title=Tradition of the Lvov-Warsaw School: Ideas and Continuations|last2=Chybińska|first2=Alicja|last3=Jadacki|first3=Jacek|last4=Woleński|first4=Jan|publisher=BRILL|year=2015|isbn=978-90-04-31175-6|location=Leiden|pages=33}}</ref>

In contemporary Polish learning, the philosopher Jan Woleński considers himself close to the School's heritage. In 2013 Woleński was awarded by the [[Foundation for Polish Science]] for his comprehensive analysis of the work of the Lwów–Warsaw school and for placing its achievements within the international discourse of contemporary [[analytic philosophy]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fnp.org.pl/en/prof-dr-hab-jan-wolenski-laureat-nagrody-fnp-2013/|title=Prof. Jan Woleński, PhD hab. – FNP Prize 2013 laureate|access-date=2016-08-11| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160319165243/http://www.fnp.org.pl/en/prof-dr-hab-jan-wolenski-laureat-nagrody-fnp-2013/| archive-date=19 March 2016}}</ref>
